title: SQL HAVING Clause
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behaviour of SQL HAVING Clause.
Write valid SQLite queries that demonstrate the topic or a documented equivalent.
Predict result rows using the supplied sample data.
Identify common mistakes and important NULL or duplicate behaviour.
Choose an appropriate query pattern for a practical reporting task.

understand.concept: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has formed them. It is commonly used with aggregate expressions such as COUNT, SUM and AVG. WHERE filters individual input rows before grouping; HAVING filters the resulting groups.
understand.whyItMatters: HAVING is useful when a report should show only customers with several orders, departments above a payroll threshold or categories whose average score meets a target.
understand.analogy: Think of a database report as carefully combining or grouping rows from well-labelled registers to answer a specific question.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL's exact evaluation rules, duplicate semantics, three-valued NULL logic or dialect-specific features.

examples.title: Show customers with at least two orders
examples.explanation: HAVING evaluates the order count for each customer group.

examples.title: Show cities whose sales exceed a threshold
examples.explanation: Only city groups whose total is greater than 150 remain.

examples.title: Combine WHERE and HAVING
examples.explanation: WHERE removes small individual orders first; HAVING then filters the remaining city totals.

examples.title: Filter groups using an average
examples.explanation: HAVING can filter groups by an average aggregate.

examples.title: Keep groups whose order count is not one
examples.explanation: The condition removes one-order customer groups.

practise.guidedTask: Run a grouped order count, then add HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2. Next add WHERE amount >= 100 before GROUP BY and compare the result.
practise.independentTask: Build a sales report grouped by sales_rep and region. Use WHERE to restrict the reporting period and HAVING to retain only groups with a minimum order count and revenue total.
hints: HAVING is applied to groups, not individual source rows.
WHERE normally cannot use aggregate functions in its condition.
HAVING can be used with aggregate expressions.
Use both clauses when row-level and group-level filters are needed.
Ensure selected non-aggregate columns are grouped.

questions.prompt: Which clause should filter individual orders before aggregation?
questions.explanation: WHERE restricts source rows before grouping.

questions.prompt: Which clause can filter groups using COUNT(*) >= 2?
questions.explanation: HAVING can apply aggregate conditions to groups.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of using WHERE amount >= 100 and HAVING SUM(amount) >= 150?
options: It filters individual orders first, then filters group totals
It filters totals before reading rows
It changes the stored amount values
It removes the GROUP BY operation
questions.answer: It filters individual orders first, then filters group totals
questions.explanation: WHERE and HAVING act at different logical stages.

questions.prompt: Can HAVING be used without an explicit GROUP BY in supported SQL engines?
options: Yes, it can apply to the single implicit aggregate group
Only in SQLite when a table is empty
questions.answer: Yes, it can apply to the single implicit aggregate group
questions.explanation: An aggregate query without GROUP BY can form one implicit group; dialect details should be checked.
